name: Isolated Sternocostoclavicular Hyperostosis

criteria.description: Radiological evidence of hyperostosis and sclerosis localized to the sternocostoclavicular region
Chronic swelling and tenderness over the sternocostoclavicular joint without systemic inflammatory signs
Exclusion of other causes such as SAPHO syndrome, infectious osteomyelitis, and malignancy
No associated psoriatic or dermatological manifestations

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of radiologic hyperostosis and chronic sternocostoclavicular swelling with exclusion of other differential diagnoses
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical and radiological; biopsy is rarely required.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Localized hyperostotic bony swelling of sternocostoclavicular joint
searchTerms: localized bone overgrowth at sternoclavicular joint

pathognomonic.symptomName: Sclerosis and hyperostosis on imaging confined to sternocostoclavicular region
searchTerms: bone thickening near sternoclavicular joint on scan
increased bone density at chest joint

common.symptomName: Chronic pain and tenderness over sternocostoclavicular joint
searchTerms: long-term pain over chest collarbone joint

common.symptomName: Soft tissue swelling around sternocostoclavicular area
searchTerms: swelling of soft tissues near chest joint

common.symptomName: Mild local warmth without systemic fever
searchTerms: slight warmth over joint without fever
mildly warm skin on affected joint

occasional.symptomName: Mild fatigue related to chronic inflammation

searchTerms: slight skin redness at affected area

rare.symptomName: Development of osteitis in adjacent ribs
searchTerms: osteitis affecting ribs adjacent to joint

laboratory: Normal or mildly elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP)
imaging: CT or X-ray showing hyperostosis and sclerosis of sternocostoclavicular joint
Bone scintigraphy showing increased uptake localized to sternocostoclavicular region
genetic: No known specific genetic mutations identified
other: Histopathology (if biopsy done) showing chronic osteitis with hyperostosis

distinguishingFeatures: Presence of skin manifestations such as pustulosis or acne
Systemic signs of infection such as fever and elevated white blood cell count

redFlags: Rapidly progressive swelling with systemic symptoms
Unexplained fever and elevated inflammatory markers
Neurological deficits suggestive of brachial plexus involvement
references: Wittekindt C, et al. Isolated sternocostoclavicular hyperostosis: clinical and radiological features. Rheumatology International. 2019.
Kahn MF, et al. Sternocostoclavicular hyperostosis: a distinct entity. Ann Rheum Dis. 1990.
